title: Correlation with your own past
objectives: Compute the lag-k autocorrelation by hand and in code, as statsmodels does
Read a correlogram against its ±1.96/√n band, and know when not to

screens.title: A copy, shifted
screens.prose: The solid line is the first 80 of 500 days of a seeded series. The dashed line is the same series moved right by $k$ days, so above day $t$ it shows $x_{t-k}$. Slide $k$ from 0 to 10 and watch the caption.

derive.caption: Shift {{k}} days: over all 500 days, $x_t$ and $x_{t-k}$ have correlation {{fixed(R[k], 2)}}

screens.question: As the shift grows, what happens to the correlation between the series and its shifted copy?

options.text: It falls quickly at first, then fades to about 0 by $k = 6$
It stays near 0.63 at every shift
options.why: You read the first shift only. Slide on to $k = 5$: the caption drops to 0.12.

options.text: It drops straight to 0 at $k = 1$
options.why: At $k = 1$ the caption reads 0.63, far from 0. Yesterday's value still says a lot about today's.

options.text: It keeps falling, down towards −1
options.why: Slide to 10: the correlation settles near 0 and never goes much below it. It shrinks, it does not flip.

hints.text: Slide one step at a time and read the caption each time.
The dashed line is the copy. Compare it with the solid line at $k = 1$, then at $k = 6$.
The caption reads 0.63, 0.38, 0.29, 0.20, 0.12, then about 0.04 at $k = 6$.

feedback.correct: That's it. The memory fades over about five days.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide from 0 to 10 and read the caption at each step.

explain.text: At $k = 1$ the two lines move together: correlation 0.63. By $k = 5$ it is 0.12, and from about $k = 6$ the copy tells us nothing. A series that correlates with its own past has **memory**, and this lesson measures it.

screens.title: Today against $k$ days ago
screens.prose: Each dot is one day of the same 500: today's value $x_t$ up the side, the value $k$ days earlier along the bottom. The line is the least squares fit, with its equation. Slide the lag.

derive.caption: Lag {{k}}: each dot is a day $t$ against day $t - k$

screens.question: Read the slope of the fitted line at lags 1, 2 and 3.

hints.text: The slope is the number in front of $x$ in the equation on the chart.
The highlighted dot is the day with the largest $x_{t-k}$. Follow the line back from it.
The equation reads 0.631 at lag 1, 0.385 at lag 2 and 0.296 at lag 3.

feedback.correct: Correct. The slope falls from 0.63 to 0.39 to 0.3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the lag, then copy the coefficient of $x$ from the equation.

explain.text: The slopes are 0.631, 0.385 and 0.296: nearly the correlations of the hook. Regressing a series on its own lag gives a slope of covariance over variance (Regression, lesson 2). For a stationary series both variances are the same, so slope and correlation agree.

screens.title: The lag-$k$ autocorrelation
screens.prose: The slope you read is the **lag-$k$ autocorrelation**. statsmodels estimates it with the full-sample mean $\bar x$ and one denominator for every lag: $$\hat\rho_k = \frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{n}(x_t - \bar x)(x_{t-k} - \bar x)}{\sum_{t=1}^{n}(x_t - \bar x)^2}.$$ Here are eight days of a spread, in pence.
screens.question: Work through $\hat\rho_1$ by hand.

hints.text: Start with the mean: the eight values add to 24.
The deviations from 3 are −1, 0, 2, 3, 1, 0, −2, −3.
Squares: 1 + 0 + 4 + 9 + 1 + 0 + 4 + 9 = 28. Neighbour products: 0, 0, 6, 3, 0, 0, 6, which add to 15. So $\hat\rho_1 = 15/28 = 0.536$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract 3 from every value, then square the deviations for the bottom and multiply neighbours for the top.

explain.text: The deviations from 3 are −1, 0, 2, 3, 1, 0, −2, −3. Their squares add to 28 and neighbouring products add to 15, so $\hat\rho_1 = 15/28 = 0.536$. One denominator over all $n$ days is why $\hat\rho_k$ differs a little from the slope of the pairs.

screens.title: The ACF in code
screens.prose: The list $\hat\rho_0, \hat\rho_1, \dots, \hat\rho_K$ is the **autocorrelation function**, the ACF. statsmodels' `acf(x, nlags=K)` returns it from lag 0, which is always 1. Its values for `make_ar1(0.6, 500, 5)` are below; match them to 6 places.
screens.question: Complete `sample_acf(x, nlags)` so it returns lags 0 to `nlags` as statsmodels does.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: the spread above, seeded series from `make_ar1(phi, n, seed)` and `make_wn(seed)` (already defined) against statsmodels' `acf` to 6 places, a shifted copy, and a series of 3 values. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: The denominator is the sum of squared deviations, used for every lag.
`d[k:]` is $x_t - \bar x$ for $t \ge k$, and `d[:-k]` the values $k$ days earlier.
`denom = np.sum(d * d)` and `out.append(np.sum(d[k:] * d[:-k]) / denom)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Your ACF matches statsmodels to 6 places.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Use the full-sample mean, and divide every lag by the same sum of squares.

explain.text: `d[k:] * d[:-k]` pairs each day with the day $k$ before it, over $n - k$ pairs. Dividing by the full sum of squares, not by $n - k$ pairs' own spread, is statsmodels' convention. It keeps the estimates stable at long lags. Adding 100 to every value changes nothing: the mean absorbs it.

screens.title: The correlogram
screens.prose: A bar chart of the ACF against the lag is a **correlogram**. Here is `make_ar1(0.6, 500, 5)` at lags 1 to 20. The series was built with $\phi = 0.6$, and its true autocorrelation is $0.6^k$, the dashed curve.
screens.question: Lags 15 to 17 reach about 0.09 to 0.10, but $0.6^{15}$ is 0.0005. What are those three bars?

options.text: Chance: an estimate from 500 days wobbles around the truth
A 15-day cycle hidden in the series
options.why: You read a pattern into three bars. The series is a seeded AR(1) with no cycle: its true lag-15 autocorrelation is $0.6^{15} = 0.0005$.

options.text: Proof the series is not stationary
options.why: A non-stationary walk keeps high bars at every lag. Here lags 6 to 14 sit near 0, so the long memory is not there.

options.text: A mistake in the ACF calculation
options.why: Your `sample_acf` matched statsmodels to 6 places. The numbers are right; they are noisy.

hints.text: How was the series made, and what is its true value at lag 15?
These three bars stand out near the end.
Lags 1 to 5 follow $0.6^k$ closely. Out at lag 15 the truth is about 0, so the bars there are estimation error.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the bars with the dashed curve: what is the true value at lag 15?

byKey.cycle: You read a cycle into three neighbouring bars. A real cycle repeats; these do not, and the truth at lag 15 is 0.0005.

explain.text: Each $\hat\rho_k$ is an estimate, so it strays from the truth by about $1/\sqrt{500} = 0.045$ either way, and neighbouring lags stray together. Lags 1 to 5 track $0.6^k$: 0.63 against 0.6, 0.38 against 0.36. Next we measure how far chance alone can push a bar.

screens.title: How far chance strays
screens.prose: Suppose a series has no memory at all. Then each $\hat\rho_k$ from $n$ days is roughly normal, with mean 0 and sd $1/\sqrt n$ (Bartlett's result). The curve is that distribution for $n = 500$: sd $0.0447$.

params.xLabel: $\hat\rho_k$ of a series with no memory

screens.question: Within what distance of 0 do 95% of these estimates fall? Give the half-width to 4 places.

hints.text: 95% of a normal lies within 1.96 sds of its mean.
The two shaded tails hold the outer 5% together.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the sd $1/\sqrt{500}$ by 1.96.

byKey.sd: You gave one sd. 95% of a normal needs 1.96 sds either side.
byKey.noroot: You divided by 500, not by $\sqrt{500}$. The sd of $\hat\rho_k$ is $1/\sqrt n$.
byKey.onesided: You used 1.645, the one-sided 5% point. A bar can stray either way, so use 1.96.

explain.text: $1.96/\sqrt{500} = 0.0877$. A series with no memory keeps 95% of its bars inside $\pm 0.0877$. This is the dashed **band** on every correlogram from here on; it shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$, so more data finds smaller effects.

screens.title: Which lags stand out
screens.prose: Turn the band into a screen for memory: list every lag whose bar lies outside it. On the AR(1) above you should find lags 1 to 5 and the three chance bars at 15 to 17.
screens.question: Complete `acf_band(n, z)` and `lags_outside_band(x, nlags)`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def acf_band(n, z=1.96):
    return ...                  # half-width of the noise band for n points

def lags_outside_band(x, nlags):
    r = sample_acf(x, nlags)    # lags 0 to nlags; sample_acf is defined for you
    b = acf_band(len(x))
    return ...                  # the lags k from 1 to nlags with |r[k]| > b
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: the band at three sizes, rounded to 4 places, and the lags outside it for seeded series from `make_ar1` and `make_wn`. `sample_acf` is your function from the last screen, already defined. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: The band is $z/\sqrt n$.
The lags run from 1 to `nlags`; lag 0 is always 1 and never counts.
`return z / np.sqrt(n)` and `return [k for k in range(1, nlags + 1) if abs(r[k]) > b]`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Lags 1 to 5 and 15 to 17 for the AR(1); none for `make_wn(3)`.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Use $z/\sqrt n$ for the band, compare $|\hat\rho_k|$ with it, and start at lag 1.

explain.text: The AR(1) gives [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 15, 16, 17]: five true lags and three by chance. White noise `make_wn(24)` gives [6, 12], with nothing behind them. A list of lags outside the band is a screen, not a verdict; lesson 6 turns it into a test.

screens.title: A walk remembers everything?
screens.prose: Bottom: the correlogram of a seeded random walk, `make_walk(4, 500)`: 0.995 at lag 1, 0.946 at lag 10. A colleague says: "Huge memory at every lag. Today's level predicts next month's, so we can trade it." Top: press New paths to draw other walks.
screens.question: What is wrong with the colleague's reading?

options.text: The walk is not stationary, so its ACF estimates no fixed quantity; its changes, the part you trade, have no memory
Nothing: an autocorrelation of 0.995 is strong evidence of predictability
options.why: You read the bars as a property of the walk. Every walk gives slow decay whatever its shocks, and the daily changes sit inside the band.

options.text: The bars are inside the band, so they mean nothing
options.why: They are far outside it: 0.995 against 0.088. The problem is what they measure, not their size.

options.text: Only lag 1 counts, so the colleague should ignore lags 2 to 20
options.why: Lag 1 is 0.995, the most misleading bar of all. The problem is the series, not the choice of lags.

hints.text: Press New paths a few times. Does each walk return to a fixed level?
The grey bars are the ACF of the daily changes.
A walk has no fixed mean or variance (level 1), so its slow decay describes nothing stable. Its changes are inside the band.

feedback.correct: That's it. Difference first, then read the ACF.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the walk has a fixed mean for the ACF to measure around.

byKey.trade: You took a high ACF as tradable memory. A walk's ACF is high by construction, and its changes, which are what you would trade, show nothing.

explain.text: A walk has no fixed mean or variance (lesson 2), so its lag-10 autocorrelation is no fixed number: seeds 5 and 6 give 0.78 and 0.83. Slow, steady decay is the unit root of lesson 3 seen through the ACF. Difference first (lesson 4): the changes have no bar outside the band.

screens.title: A weekly pattern
screens.prose: Lesson 4's seeded daily volume, `make_volume(91)`: 300 trading days, busy on Mondays and Fridays and quiet midweek. Its correlogram has a band of $\pm 0.113$ for $n = 300$.
screens.question: Tap the lags that are a whole number of weeks apart.

hints.text: A trading week has 5 days.
Same weekday, one week apart: lag 5.
Lags 5, 10, 15 and 20 pair each day with the same weekday, and their bars are the tallest, about 0.7.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the lags that pair a Monday with a Monday.

byKey.neg: You tapped the deep negative bars. Those pair a busy day with a quiet one; the weekly lags are the tall positive ones.

explain.text: Every fifth lag pairs a Monday with a Monday, so the bars at 5, 10, 15 and 20 are about 0.7. Lags 2 and 3 pair busy days with quiet ones, so they are strongly negative. A seasonal series shows its period as a comb of spikes; the seasonal difference of lesson 4 removes it.

screens.title: The ACF and its band
screens.prose: You lined a series up against its own past and read the slope. That is $$\hat\rho_k = \frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{n}(x_t - \bar x)(x_{t-k} - \bar x)}{\sum_{t=1}^{n}(x_t - \bar x)^2}, \qquad \text{band} = \pm\frac{1.96}{\sqrt n}.$$ A bar outside the band is memory that pure noise would show only 5% of the time. Read it only on a stationary series.
screens.question: Where is the band on a correlogram of 1,000 days?

options.why: You divided 1.96 by 1,000. The band shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$, so divide by $\sqrt{1000} = 31.6$.
That is the band for 500 days. With twice the data it narrows by $\sqrt 2$, to 0.062.
That is one sd, $1/\sqrt{1000}$. The 95% band is 1.96 times it.

explain.text: $1.96/\sqrt{1000} = 1.96/31.6 = 0.062$. Quadrupling the data halves the band.

screens.title: Index returns
screens.prose: A stylised fact (Tsay, chapter 2): the daily returns of a broad index have lag-1 autocorrelation close to 0. Here is a seeded stand-in, the log returns of `make_price(12)`: 1,999 days, band $\pm 0.044$. Every bar is inside it; the largest is −0.041 at lag 11.
screens.question: A trader proposes buying after an up day. What does the correlogram say?

options.text: Today's return says almost nothing, linearly, about tomorrow's
Lag 1 is positive, so the rule earns about 1.6% a day
options.why: You read the bar's height as a return. $\hat\rho_1 = 0.016$ is a correlation, inside the band, and could easily be 0.

options.text: The bars are mostly negative, so selling after up days works
options.why: Small negative bars inside the band are what noise draws. None of them is evidence of reversal.

options.text: Returns cannot be predicted in any way at all
options.why: The ACF only sees linear memory in returns. Their size is predictable (lesson 6), which is the GARCH course.

hints.text: Is any bar outside the dashed band?
Lag 1 is the bar the trader is betting on.
$\hat\rho_1 = 0.016$, well inside $\pm 0.044$: no detectable linear memory.

feedback.correct: Correct. No bar leaves the band.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check where the lag-1 bar sits against the band.

byKey.neg: You treated a correlation of 0.016 as a return. It is inside the band, so we cannot tell it from 0.

explain.text: Every bar is inside $\pm 0.044$, so the data show no linear memory at daily lags. This stand-in was built as a random walk, so that is true by construction; real index returns look much the same. It is the efficient-markets reading lesson 6 makes precise.

screens.title: The bid-ask bounce
screens.prose: A share quotes a 2p spread around its mid-price, which moves with sd 0.3p from trade to trade. Each trade prints at the bid or the ask, mid ± 1p, on a fair coin (Microstructure, lesson 1). The chart shows 40 of 1,000 seeded trades, in pence.
screens.question: What is the lag-1 autocorrelation of the trade-to-trade price changes, roughly?

options.text: About −0.5
About 0, because the mid is a random walk
options.why: You looked at the mid only. Each print adds a bid-or-ask jump that the next print tends to undo.

options.text: About +0.5
options.why: A jump up to the ask is usually followed by a print at the bid, a fall. Neighbouring changes have opposite signs.

options.text: About −1
options.why: That would need the next change to undo the last one exactly. The mid moves too, and some prints repeat the same side.

hints.text: After a print at the ask, where is the next print likely to be?
The thin line jumps up and down around the mid.
Write the change as the mid move plus $s(q_t - q_{t-1})$ with $q_t = \pm 1$. Its lag-1 covariance is $-s^2$ and its variance $\sigma_m^2 + 2s^2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what follows a print at the ask.

byKey.zero: You used the mid's memory. The traded price adds a bounce whose changes are negatively correlated.

explain.text: With $s = 1$p and $\sigma_m = 0.3$p, $\rho_1 = -s^2/(\sigma_m^2 + 2s^2) = -1/2.09 = −0.478$; the 1,000 seeded trades give −0.451. Mid-price changes give −0.009. A negative lag-1 autocorrelation in trade prices is the bounce, not mean reversion you can trade.

ideas: The lag-$k$ autocorrelation $\hat\rho_k$ compares a series with itself $k$ days earlier. It is nearly the slope of $x_t$ on $x_{t-k}$.
A series with no memory keeps 95% of its bars inside $\pm 1.96/\sqrt n$. One bar in twenty leaves it by chance.
Read the ACF only on a stationary series. A random walk's bars decay slowly whatever its shocks; difference it first.

formula.name: Sample autocorrelation
formula.note: Full-sample mean, one denominator for every lag: the convention of `statsmodels.tsa.stattools.acf`.

summary.trap: High bars on a price chart are not tradable memory: a random walk's ACF decays slowly by construction.

quiz.prose: A new fund has 20 days of returns, and their lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.30.
quiz.question: How wide is the 95% band for 20 days, to 2 places?

byKey.sd: You gave one sd, $1/\sqrt{20}$. The band is 1.96 times it.

explain.text: $1.96/\sqrt{20} = 0.44$. With 20 days almost nothing is significant: 0.30 could be pure noise.

quiz.prose: A spread series is quoted in pence. A colleague adds 50p to every value to remove negative numbers.
quiz.question: What happens to its ACF?

options.text: Nothing changes
Every $\hat\rho_k$ rises towards 1
options.why: You expected the level to add memory. $\hat\rho_k$ uses deviations from the mean, and the 50p moves the mean too.

options.text: It scales by 50
options.why: Autocorrelations have no units. They are ratios of sums of products of deviations.

feedback.correct: Correct. The mean absorbs the shift.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what $x_t - \bar x$ does when every value rises by 50.

explain.text: Every $x_t - \bar x$ is unchanged when all values rise by 50p, so every $\hat\rho_k$ is too.

quiz.prose: Ten years of daily returns, 2,500 days, give $\hat\rho_1 = 0.05$. The band is $\pm 0.039$.
quiz.question: Which reading is right?

options.text: It is outside the band, but it explains only about 0.25% of the variance
It is inside the band, so it is noise
options.why: Compare again: 0.05 is larger than 0.039, so it is outside.

options.text: It is outside the band, so it is a strong, tradable effect
options.why: Outside the band means detectable, not large. $0.05^2 = 0.0025$ of the variance, before costs.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 0.05 with 0.039, then square 0.05.

explain.text: With 2,500 days the band is narrow, so 0.05 is detectable. But a lag-1 correlation of 0.05 explains $0.05^2 = 0.25\%$ of tomorrow's variance, which costs can easily eat.

quiz.prose: You draw the correlogram of 750 daily closes of a share. It starts at 0.99 and falls almost in a straight line to 0.80 at lag 20.
quiz.question: What should you do first?

options.text: Difference the closes, or take log returns, and look again
Fit a model with 20 lags to capture the memory
options.why: You read slow decay as memory to model. It is the signature of a unit root, which the ACF cannot measure.

options.text: Nothing: every bar is outside the band, so the memory is real
options.why: Outside the band is not the point here. A walk's bars are high whatever its shocks.

feedback.correct: Correct. Slow decay says unit root: difference first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What did the random walk's correlogram look like?

explain.text: Slow, steady decay from near 1 is how a unit root looks in the ACF. Prices are not stationary; returns are. Difference first, then read the correlogram.
